claims.statement: Barbegal's repeated seasonal interruptions support a variable operating schedule; ship's biscuit production is a plausible but unconfirmed market explanation.

sources.locator: Results: Stable isotope composition, Fig. 4; Discussion
sources.supports: Truncated seasonal sequences and the authors' hardtack interpretation.

claims.counterevidence: Water availability, other seasonal markets, or other operating choices might also produce pauses.
claims.inference_limits: The carbonate records do not identify the product's final consumer.

test.mechanism_chain: Seasonal shipping demand -> mill managers schedule production -> recurrent late-summer/autumn pauses.
test.strongest_rival: Seasonal water limits or a different flour market could cause the same schedule.
test.discriminating_observation: Independent seasonal water reconstruction plus securely associated baking, storage, shipment or purchasing records.
test.evidence_sought_found: ANC-S03 isotope results and alternative-market discussion inspected; no direct customer record.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Production purpose is inferred from timing and location; alternatives not eliminated.

claims.statement: Frontinus reports about 240 publicly owned and 460 imperial enslaved aqueduct workers organised into specialised maintenance functions.
claims.counterevidence: His account also complains about diversion of workers to private tasks.
claims.inference_limits: High confidence in the reported arrangement, not an independently verified staffing census.

test.reason: Attribution to a specific ancient account, with performance limits explicit.

claims.statement: Polybius reports that earlier Persian rulers offered five generations of cultivation rights for bringing water to unirrigated land; the inspected translation does not explicitly state a tax exemption.

sources.supports: Reported incentive and expense in Paton's wording.
Critical contextualisation of the reported galleries.

claims.counterevidence: Other translations or legal interpretations may construe the benefit differently.
claims.inference_limits: Local retrospective testimony is not an actual grant deed or proof of universal enforcement.

test.reason: Exact attribution to a transmitted report and its inspected translation; investment causation is separately hypothetical.

claims.statement: A gravity-fed groundwater gallery can supply its outlet only when water is available at a compatible elevation and the channel remains passable; knowing the technique alone does not establish local feasibility.

sources.supports: Geometry of gallery supply and locally adjusted depth.

claims.counterevidence: Pumped or surface-fed supply can replace the service, but constitutes a different configuration.
claims.inference_limits: Physical constraint, not a historical cost model or estimate of aquifer sustainability.

test.mechanism_chain: Accessible groundwater and gradient -> gravity flow through a passable gallery -> outlet supply.
test.strongest_rival: An apparently similar tunnel may instead convey an external surface source.
test.discriminating_observation: Trace the collecting section, outlet elevations and water source; distinguish groundwater interception from conveyance.
test.evidence_sought_found: ANC-S08 explicitly separates gallery types and water sources.
test.remaining_ambiguity: The physical relationship is clear; source classification of particular early galleries remains disputed.

sources.title: The second century CE Roman watermills of Barbegal: Unraveling the enigma of one of the oldest industrial complexes
sources.locator: Science Advances 4(9), eaar3620. Introduction; Results: microstratigraphy, crystal structure, stable isotope composition; Fig. 4; Discussion. Full article XML acquired at https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC6124920/fullTextXML after publisher/PMC browser access failed.
sources.scope_limit: Carbonate samples record selected structures and years. Seasonal interruptions are better supported than identification of customers or hardtack production. Wider claims about Roman growth and empire-wide crises are not independently established here.
sources.evidence_lineage: Original analysis of carbonate fragments from the 1930s Barbegal excavations, surviving museum material and site evidence. ANC-S04 reanalyses overlapping material; the two papers are not independent replications.

sources.title: The Aqueducts of Rome (De aquaeductu urbis Romae), Book II
sources.locator: Ancient account c. 97–early second century CE; Loeb English edition. Inspected §§94–96, 116–129, especially §§116–118 (workforce and funding), 121–124 (repair scheduling and access).
sources.scope_limit: Official self-presentation and prescriptions are not audited performance records. Reported staffing and finances are for Rome at a particular time, not the entire empire. Translation uses 'wages' for expenses of enslaved gangs; this does not establish free contractual employment.
sources.evidence_lineage: Transmitted text by an imperial water commissioner, including quoted earlier legal measures. Bannon (ANC-S06) uses this same source alongside inscriptions and juristic texts; overlapping propositions are not independent corroboration.

sources.title: Qanāt and Falaj: Polycentric and Multi-Period Innovations: Iran and the United Arab Emirates as Case Studies
sources.locator: Underground Aqueducts Handbook, chapter 17, pp. 279–301; inspected chapter OCR, especially §§17.1–17.2.3 (pp. 280–288) and §§17.3.4–17.4.2 (pp. 293–295).
sources.scope_limit: Archaeological synthesis with explicit disagreements, including shallow versus deeper sources and early Iranian dating. Most underlying excavation reports and luminescence datasets were not acquired. Polycentric origins are argued, not established at every site.
sources.evidence_lineage: Author's comparative archaeological interpretation, drawing on excavations at al-Madam and other UAE sites plus previous Iranian studies. Its treatment of Polybius overlaps ANC-S09; chronology is not an independent dataset for every repeated later citation.

sources.title: Histories, Book X, chapter 28
sources.locator: X.28.1–7, especially §§2–4; Loeb volume IV, pp. 169–171. Describes Antiochus III's Parthian campaign, conventionally 209 BCE, from a later second-century BCE account.
sources.scope_limit: Reports local testimony about earlier Persian rule; not an original grant or construction account. Paton's wording is five generations of cultivation rights, not an explicit tax exemption. The water source is not technically specified. Host notes this page is not fully proofread.
sources.evidence_lineage: Single ancient transmitted narrative. Boucharlat (ANC-S08) critically interprets the same passage. Reading both does not give two independent witnesses to the grant policy.

cases.title: Barbegal's watermill complex: seasonal operation and staged cessation
cases.period: Second–third centuries CE; terminal reconstruction concerns selected western mills' final roughly 8–9 years
cases.summary: Material traces establish operating watermills and changes in equipment; market destination and final abandonment cause remain uncertain.

stages.invention: No first-invention claim; the case concerns an installation.
stages.feasibility: Operational deposits and architecture support repeated use.
stages.deployment: Sixteen wheel positions in two trains; selected surviving casts.
stages.diffusion: No regional denominator; Barbegal does not establish commonness.
stages.scaling: Substantial integrated capacity, without adopted output tonnage.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Seasonal operation inferred; possible ship-biscuit market not confirmed.
stages.displacement/reversal: Different western flumes ceased in stages while water continued; later reuse occurs.

mechanisms: Water infrastructure and machinery complement one another.
Repair preserves capacity; water availability alone is insufficient.
Demand and seasonal operating schedules may interact.
cases.counterevidence: Shared carbonate archive limits independence of studies; discharge, markets, ownership and the eastern train's exact fate are incompletely known.

episode.technology_configuration: Two trains of eight aqueduct-powered wheels; terminal evidence specifically from three western flumes.
episode.task: Grinding grain; final consumer and possible biscuit manufacture uncertain.
episode.population: Operators and consumers of this installation, identities and number unknown.
episode.interval: Second–third centuries CE, with distinct terminal subepisodes per flume.
contemporary_alternatives: Hand, animal and smaller watermills as contemporaneous technological alternatives; no evidence the owner explicitly priced and rejected them.
episode.adoption_measure: Installation configuration plus sampled isotope/microstratigraphic sequences. No population of eligible mills or percentage adoption.
episode.observation_limits: Wood decayed; carbonate preserves selected parts and years. Wheel positions are not year-round output.

actors.payer: Financing and ownership unknown; substantial construction does not identify public or private payer.
actors.operator_maintainer: Milling and woodworking/repair workers implied by physical interventions; legal status and pay unknown.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Potential grain suppliers, consumers and workers, but identities and distributions not recovered.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Unknown for Barbegal workers; Roman slavery elsewhere cannot determine their status.

labour.tasks: Grinding energy supplied by water; grain handling, millstone care, woodworking and flume adjustment persisted. Net labour change unmeasured.
labour.entry_barriers: Access to an appropriate supply/fall, machinery and repair competence; entry cost not quantified.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Ownership and allocation of saved effort or revenue unknown.
labour.transition: Years of component replacement are visible; worker biographies or displacement duration are not.
labour.distribution: No observed wages, consumption distribution or compensation for displaced millers.
labour.evidence_limit: Capacity cannot be translated into employment eliminated or general emancipation from labour.

cases.title: Rome's aqueduct service and the 537 milling emergency
cases.period: Subepisode A: c. 97–early second century CE maintenance administration; subepisode B: siege of 537 CE
cases.summary: Administrative evidence makes maintenance, funding and allocation visible; a later siege narrative describes different outcomes for drinking, bathing and milling.

stages.feasibility: Established urban conduits and mills, not just technical descriptions.
stages.deployment: Frontinus describes Rome's services and workforce; Procopius describes mills dependent on an aqueduct.
stages.diffusion: No inference from Rome to every Roman city.
stages.scaling: Maintenance and distribution arrangements support a large service; exact consumption not reconstructed.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Animal-driven substitution reportedly restricted by fodder shortage in 537; wells remained useful.
stages.displacement/reversal: Siege interruption and reported boatmill replacement; not proof of permanent universal aqueduct loss.

mechanisms: Recurrent finance, workforce, access and repair schedules complement physical assets.
Emergency substitution depends on resources required by each alternative.
cases.counterevidence: Frontinus is prescriptive and self-presentational; Procopius is a single later narrative. The two subepisodes cannot be treated as one continuous panel.

episode.technology_configuration: A: aqueduct maintenance/distribution at Rome. B: aqueduct-fed Janiculum mills and reported Tiber boatmills during siege.
episode.task: A: reliable water delivery and allocation. B: grinding during blockade, distinguished from drinking and bathing.
episode.population: A: officials, enslaved work gangs and entitled water users. B: siege population and military organisers; exact coverage unknown.
episode.interval: Two explicitly separate episodes, c. 100 and 537 CE.
contemporary_alternatives: Wells and river for drinking, attested by Procopius.
Animal milling was a known but fodder-constrained option in 537.
Tiber boatmills reportedly substituted during siege.
episode.adoption_measure: Textual staffing and procedural account; narrative emergency sequence. No quantified diffusion or service-coverage denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Reported rules differ from enforcement; staffing is not employment trend; narrative sufficiency is not throughput.

actors.chooser: A: water commissioner, emperor and other authorities in defined legal roles. B: Belisarius according to Procopius.
actors.payer: A: public treasury, imperial purse and some water-right revenue. B: funds and requisition arrangements not specified.
actors.operator_maintainer: A: public/imperial enslaved specialists and contractors. B: boatmill builders/operators not individually identified.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Enslaved workers; water users without decision authority; households dependent on distributions; siege residents.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Enslaved maintenance workers did not have ordinary free-labour choice; precise coercion and resistance not measured. Household alternatives varied; siege constrained choice.

labour.tasks: Inspection, cleaning, masonry, piping and administration; boatmill assembly and tending in 537. Enslaved labour explicitly present in A.
labour.entry_barriers: Specialised work roles and controlled access to assets; actual training pathways unknown.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Public/imperial ownership and grants shape control; individual worker bargaining power unmeasured.
labour.transition: No linked worker cohorts across the two widely separated episodes.
labour.distribution: Access was differentiated legally; no quantified welfare or wage change by group.
labour.evidence_limit: Do not infer freedom, consent or secure livelihoods from useful infrastructure; no employment multiplier calculated.

cases.title: Early southeast Arabian falaj with an Iranian textual contrast
region: Southeast Arabia, especially al-Madam and Al Ain (present UAE)
cases.period: Arabian first millennium BCE; Iranian channels described for a late third-century BCE campaign; later revival mentioned only as a contrast
cases.summary: Local galleries show adaptation and limits. A separate Iranian narrative reports a long benefit horizon, without establishing a shared origin or universal governance system.

stages.invention: Multiple-origin and diffusion hypotheses remain contested.
stages.feasibility: Groundwater interception plus suitable gradient differs from mere underground conveyance.
stages.deployment: Excavated Arabian installations associated with settlements; Iranian account is textual.
stages.diffusion: No universal direction or adoption denominator established.
stages.scaling: Regional settlement associations are not a quantified output expansion.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Conditions and source depths vary; wells remain a named alternative in the synthesis.
stages.displacement/reversal: Deepening and later silting/abandonment at al-Madam; later deep galleries are not assumed a direct continuous lineage.

mechanisms: Groundwater and gradient constrain feasible operation.
Durable benefit rights could encourage investment, but that causal reading is untested.
cases.counterevidence: Poor dating and excavation in Iran can distort apparent priority; similar gallery forms fit diffusion plus adaptation as well as independent innovation.

episode.technology_configuration: A: early Arabian shafts-and-gallery water catchment, with al-Madam alteration sequence. B: northern Iranian underground channels in Polybius, water source not specified.
episode.task: Bring water to settlement/cultivation; in Polybius also water access on a military route.
episode.population: A: excavated settlements' users. B: people reported as beneficiaries of earlier Persian cultivation grants; no census.
episode.interval: Distinct regional episodes within the first millennium BCE.
contemporary_alternatives: Surface-water channels where an appropriate source exists; unavailable at some sites rather than demonstrably rejected.
episode.adoption_measure: Archaeological occurrence and local relative sequence, plus one narrative report. No number of eligible settlements or diffusion rate.
episode.observation_limits: Many galleries undated or repeatedly altered; collecting and conveying functions can be confused; written and excavated populations differ.

actors.chooser: Arabian builders and allocation authorities incompletely identified; Persian rulers reported as grantors in a separate literary story.
actors.payer: Arabian financing unknown; Polybius reports substantial expense by builders but gives no accounts.
actors.operator_maintainer: Diggers, cleaners and water users required; named people, remuneration and labour status unknown in these ancient episodes.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Dependent cultivators and downstream/competing users are plausible affected groups, not measured participants.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Unknown: later communal water rules cannot be projected onto first-millennium BCE settlements.

labour.tasks: Excavation, depth adjustment, clearing and water distribution; reduced recurring lift at a suitable gravity outlet is a physical inference, not measured net labour saving.
labour.entry_barriers: Local water-location, gradient-setting and excavation knowledge; access rights and capital may matter but are not quantified.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Polybius's cultivation right is reported; actual title, inheritance conditions and division of benefits unknown.
labour.transition: Physical adaptation sequence known through synthesis; no individual livelihood transitions.
labour.distribution: No ancient distribution of work, water, land or surplus by group established.
labour.evidence_limit: Do not infer egalitarian community organisation, free work or indefinite sustainability from a gravity-fed design.

edges.qualification: Seasonal demand is a candidate explanation for an operating schedule, not established customer identity.

scope.configuration: Possible demand for stored ship provisions near Arles.

alternatives: Other flour markets; supply-driven seasonal stoppages.
edges.dispute: Hardtack inference lacks direct associated purchaser or product evidence.

edges.qualification: Frontinus reports this workforce; realised effectiveness not independently audited.

scope.configuration: Specialist gangs assigned to Rome's conduits and distribution.

alternatives: Contractors also performed work; other organisational forms possible.
edges.dispute: Reported staffing and duties are not a worker-day series.

edges.qualification: Only groundwater-intercepting, gravity-fed galleries; not all structures called qanat/falaj.

scope.configuration: Collecting section must intercept water high enough to feed outlet by gravity.

alternatives: Wells with lifting, surface diversion or relocation can supply water by other configurations.
edges.necessity_rationale: Without available water and a compatible hydraulic gradient, this passive gallery cannot deliver the specified outlet flow.
edges.dispute: Groundwater source and depth of some early galleries are contested.

edges.qualification: An incentive pathway suggested by Polybius's report, not verified causal identification.

scope.configuration: Long cultivation rights associated with expensive water provision in local testimony.

alternatives: Political command, inherited local rights or collective finance could organise construction.
edges.dispute: No original grant, enforcement record or comparison group; translation does not explicitly say tax exemption.
